sentences.text: Unlike most other diplodocoids, Lingwulong possessed a U-shaped snout.
This respectable-sized sauropod reached 17 meters in length, 4.5 meters in height, and weighed 15 tonnes.

Unique traits distinguishing it include elaborate ornamentation along the upper orbital margin, a transversely wide occipital condyle, and anterior dorsal vertebrae with twisted metapophyses featuring a sub-circular pseudofacet.
It stands as the oldest known neosauropod and the only definitive diplodocoid found in East Asia.
A sheep herder named Ma Yun discovered the dinosaur bones in 2004.
After finding the remains, he notified local administrators Yang Huozhu and Liu Hongan.
Excavations at Ciyaopu near Lingwu from 2005 onwards revealed remains from about seven to ten sauropod skeletons.

The species Lingwulong shenqi was named and described in 2018 by a team led by Xu Xing, Paul Upchurch, Philip D. Mannion, Paul M. Barrett, Omar R. Regalado-Fernández, Mo Jinyou, Ma Jinfu, and Liu Hongan.
Lingwulong is one of the earliest known neosauropods and the only definitive diplodocoid found in East Asia.
Lingwulong belongs to the class Saurischia.
The parent group of Lingwulong is Flagellicaudata.
Lingwulong is included in the cladogram of Flagellicaudata as presented by Xu and colleagues in 2018.
Recent 2025 analyses suggest Lingwulong is a sister taxon to Cetiosauriscus, potentially outside the Flagellicaudata clade or within Diplodocidae.
Lingwulong lived during the early to middle Jurassic, approximately 178 to 168 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
Lingwulong lived in China during the Early or Middle Jurassic period within the Yanan Formation.
Its exact age is uncertain, but it lived between the late Toarcian and Bajocian, with an estimated midpoint age of 174 million years.
Research dating the Yanan Formation suggests Lingwulong lived between 174.0 and 171.7 million years ago.
The time range for Lingwulong is from the Aalenian to the Callovian, between 174.7 and 161.5 million years ago.
Some researchers argue the fossils came from the Zhiluo Formation, which would make Lingwulong younger, dating to the Bathonian to early Oxfordian.
The presence of Lingwulong challenges the East Asian Isolation Hypothesis, suggesting diplodocoids were present in East Asia during the Jurassic.
